title: Logo for Musée de la Romanité in Nîmes
description: A minimalist logo for the Musée de la Romanité in Nîmes, set against a light gray background. The mark features a large dark navy rectangular block on the left, followed by three identical arches that resemble classical Roman architecture. Below the mark, the museum name is set in a clean, dark navy sans-serif typeface, with 'MUSÉE DE LA ROMANITÉ' on the top line and '— NIMES' on the bottom line, right-aligned. The composition is balanced and modern, with a strong geometric feel.

title: Bright Two-Level Loft Apartment
description: A sunlit two-level loft apartment with a mezzanine sleeping area. The lower level features a living space with a blue wooden sofa, a small patterned rug, and a black modern chair. Behind the sofa, the dining area has a table with white and yellow chairs. The white mezzanine, with a metal railing, displays two landscape paintings and several small plants. A long green vine trails down the left wall. The kitchen is visible in the background, and the room has light hardwood floors and white walls.

title: Six-column artist CV and portfolio text layout
description: A black-and-white typographic layout resembling a professional CV or portfolio page. The design is structured into six narrow columns under a single header row. Each column is headed by a category in all-caps, followed by a list of entries including names, locations, and years. The text is small and dense, set in a clean sans-serif font. A thin black line separates the columns, and a footer bar at the bottom contains navigation links.
ocr:
BIOGRAPHY
DANIEL GILLBERG (1978), known as EKTA, is a Swedish artist, currently based in Gothenburg.
His works have been exhibited all over Europe, as well as Japan, USA and New Zealand and can be found across the continent in collections in America, Japan, China, Poland and England.
He has recently worked on several painting exhibitions and public mural participation in Sweden. In 2013 he was awarded an artist grant from Konstnärsnämnden.
E K T A is represented by Galleri Duse in Göteborg and Minà Gallery in Berlin.

title: Geometric composition with central black circle
description: A hard-edge geometric abstract composition centered on a large black circle. The circle is flanked by vertical color blocks: a blue rectangle over a yellow square on the left, and a red rectangle over a green square on the right. Above and below the central circle are symmetrical, triangular arrangements of small, repetitive black vertical bars that taper inward toward the circle. The background is off-white.

title: DA BREAK Let It Shine Album Back Cover
description: Album back cover for a record titled 'DA BREAK'. A solid periwinkle blue background features a track listing and credits in a black sans-serif font on the left side. The right side is dominated by large, black, stylized, blocky letterforms that vertically span almost the entire height of the cover. A barcode and small logos for sponsors and labels appear at the bottom left.

title: Mid-century modern living room with large bookshelf wall
description: A spacious living room with a floor-to-ceiling wooden shelving unit covering the left wall, filled with numerous books and decorative objects. A large, dark television is mounted below the shelves, flanked by tall, thin speakers. The room features a variety of mid-century modern furniture, including a dark leather sofa, wooden coffee tables, and several armchairs.

title: Abstract and photographic gallery wall in a minimalist living room
description: A gallery wall of six framed art pieces arranged in two rows above a white sideboard. The largest piece on the left is a bold, abstract composition in orange, black, and white. Other frames include a small text-based print, a dark landscape, and several black-and-white photographs. The white sideboard holds books and small objects, and two grey chairs with wood frames flank a dark, live-edge wood coffee table. A floor lamp and a vase of dark foliage add to the modern, minimalist feel.
ocr: ARTnews

title: Living Room with Garden View Through Grid Windows
description: A warm, modern living room viewed through a large, black-framed grid window wall that reveals a lush, green garden outside. The interior features an olive green curved sofa, a matching armchair, a dark red armchair, and a dark green ottoman on a light-colored round rug. The space is illuminated by a multi-globe brass chandelier and floor lamps. The walls have elegant white paneling, and the floor is a light herringbone wood.

title: Modern Lakeside Living Room with Vaulted Wood Ceiling
description: A modern, open-plan living room with a dramatic, double-height vaulted ceiling clad in light wood planks, supported by dark beams and featuring a skylight. A large, textured wood burl sculpture is mounted on a white soffit above. The space is anchored by a large shag rug, a low-profile light grey sectional sofa with dark pillows, and a black cylindrical fireplace. Floor-to-ceiling glass walls frame a panoramic view of a calm body of water and distant hills.

title: Mid-Century Modern Living Room with Blue Seating and Wood Walls
description: Interior of a mid-century modern living room with an open floor plan and expansive glass walls looking out into a wooded backyard. The room is constructed primarily from warm, honey-toned wood, including the ceiling, floor-to-ceiling built-in shelving, and structural beams. A large, sunken seating area is arranged on an olive-green shag rug, featuring deep blue upholstered sectional sofas, matching ottomans, and a set of tan leather floor cushions in the immediate foreground.

title: Modern Living Room with Cacti and Wood Paneling
description: A modern, light-filled living and office space with a mix of organic and geometric forms. A low-profile light grey sectional sofa sits on a beige rug, backed by a light wood credenza. To the left, two large potted cacti stand near floor-to-ceiling sheer white curtains. A dark blue rectangular coffee table holds a stack of books. To the right, a wooden desk with an X-frame base and black office chairs is paired with a yellow chair.

title: Modern studio with timber ceiling and central table
description: A bright, modern office or studio space with a prominent exposed timber ceiling structure of beams and joists. A long, light wood dining-style table with black legs and wooden chairs sits centrally. Along the right wall is a workspace with a long white desk, multiple black ergonomic office chairs, a computer monitor, and overhead wooden shelving filled with books and binders. The left wall features large windows with blinds, a built-in bookshelf packed with books, and a large leafy green plant.

title: Sunlit Loft Workspace with Shelving and Sculpture
description: A person sits on a black Eames-style chair at a white desk, facing a computer monitor and holding a tablet. The room is a bright loft with large, multi-paned windows on the left. Behind the desk, white shelving holds books, framed art, and two wine bottles. A black wall clock hangs above the monitor. To the right, two motorcycle helmets rest on a white cabinet, and a refrigerator is covered in photographs and magnets.

title: Rustic Wood Bedroom with Antler Wall Display
description: A bedroom with a rustic, cabin-like aesthetic dominated by warm wood tones. The walls, ceiling, and structural beams are clad in natural wood planks. A bed with neutral bedding is centered against a back wall featuring two large panels decorated with a collection of deer antlers mounted in a scattered pattern. To the left, a large window allows natural light to enter, and a white, modern, shell-shaped chair sits nearby. A low wooden bench at the foot of the bed holds a stack of books.

title: Industrial Loft with Floor-to-Ceiling Curtains and Plants
description: A spacious, multi-level industrial loft converted into a bright, minimalist living space. The room features high, exposed concrete ceilings and walls with large, arched windows that flood the interior with soft, diffused light through sheer, floor-to-ceiling white curtains. The layout includes a lower lounge area with white modular sofas, low coffee tables, and a long wooden console table displaying artwork and decor.

title: Industrial Loft Living Space with Built-in Bookshelf
description: An industrial loft living space with polished concrete floors and exposed wooden ceiling beams joined by black steel plates. A wall of built-in wooden shelving and drawers is packed with books on the left. A large red patterned rug sits in front of the shelves, and another striped rug is partially visible in the foreground. To the right, a sofa with white, orange, and black-and-white patterned pillows is paired with a vintage trunk side table.

title: Mid-century modern living room with wooden paneling
description: A warm, mid-century modern living room with vertical wooden wall paneling and a high ceiling. A steep wooden ladder with metal rails leads to a mezzanine level with bookshelves. A person sits at a white tulip table in the background. Large floor-to-ceiling windows and glass doors look out onto a lush garden, with a red-framed sliding door open. A grey sofa and a wooden rocking chair with beige cushions occupy the foreground, alongside two small red nesting tables.

title: Mid-Century Library Corner with Brass Cabinet
description: A mid-century modern library corner with floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves filled with books. A patterned lounge chair sits centrally, facing a low, organic-shaped wooden coffee table holding a ceramic bowl. To the right, a sleek brass cabinet is mounted above more shelves. The room features a geometric black and gold rug, a red velvet ottoman, and a multi-arm black floor lamp.

title: Crowsflight navigation app design mockup
description: A design mockup showing a navigation app called Crowsflight on a smartphone. Two hand-held iPhone screenshots are stacked vertically. The top image shows the phone against a blurred city street background, while the bottom image shows it against a blurred cobblestone background. The app features a minimalist interface with a large circular compass and a bright yellow directional wedge pointing toward a destination.

title: Eclectic Living Room with Warm Ambient Lighting
description: A cozy living room with a plush, dark green velvet sofa and matching ottoman. A tall white bookshelf is filled with books and topped with a large potted plant. The room is illuminated by warm, orange-hued light from a tall floor lamp with a pleated shade, a small table lamp with a mushroom-shaped shade, and a glowing spherical lamp on a glass coffee table. A large window with a blueish dusk light is visible, along with a wooden sideboard holding a record player and a framed picture.

title: Sunlit interior with plants, shelves, and stacked containers
description: A densely packed interior space illuminated by sunlight streaming through large grid-paned windows. The scene is filled with various objects: leafy green plants climb and hang, while tables and shelves hold numerous containers, including white buckets and colorful crates in blue and orange. The floor appears to be concrete, with some equipment like wheeled carts or stands visible. The overall palette is dominated by natural light, muted earthy tones, and pops of color from the containers.
ocr: JORD USA

title: Modern Kitchen with Gallery Wall and Wood Island
description: A bright, modern kitchen with a high, pitched ceiling featuring two skylights. A long, left wall is covered in a dense, salon-style gallery of framed black-and-white photographs and prints, mostly in black frames, with one prominent orange frame. The kitchen cabinetry is built-in, with white tall units on the left and warm, medium-toned wood for the island and lower cabinets. A wooden island with drawers sits in the center, with a bowl of produce on top.

title: Industrial Loft Living and Dining Space
description: A spacious, industrial-style living and dining area with a double-height ceiling. The left side features a large, multi-paned window wall, through which a dark, enclosed courtyard with plants is visible. A black leather Eames lounge chair and ottoman sit near the window. In the foreground is a low, dark coffee table with a teapot set. The dining area has a long, light wood table with a matching bench.

title: Minimalist tour dates poster for A Special Night with Peder
description: A minimalist black-and-white concert tour poster with a clean, centered layout on a white background. The top reads 'LIDO PRESENTS' above 'A Special Night with Peder'. The main body lists ten North American cities and dates in a simple, bold sans-serif font, from San Diego on October 5th to Chicago on October 31st. The vertical margins contain 'www.lidogotsang.com' text, and the bottom shows 'October 2019 North America' flanking a small audio waveform graphic.

title: White Staircase in Converted Loft
description: A high-ceilinged loft space converted from an industrial structure, dominated by a stark white, straight-run staircase ascending from the lower left to a mezzanine. The palette contrasts cool grey concrete and white painted surfaces with warm wood tones from the mezzanine floor and ceiling planks. Sheer white curtains frame tall, arched windows, diffusing bright natural light. The mezzanine holds a glass-topped table and wire-frame chairs.

title: MiN New York Astronomy Domine Perfume Bottle
description: A small, clear glass perfume bottle with a heavy, dark, textured cap. The bottle is filled with a dark, opaque black liquid. A white rectangular label on the front has black text that reads 'MiN NEW YORK scent stories vol. 3/ch. 02 eau de parfum 15ml 0.5 fl oz'. Below this, the words 'ASTRONOMY DOMINE' are printed in a contrasting copper-colored serif font. The overall aesthetic is minimalist, stark, and modern.

title: Diane Davies freelance proofreader website design
description: A long, scrolling webpage design for a freelance proofreader named Diane Davies. The layout is minimal and text-heavy, with a prominent monogram 'Dd' at the top. The primary column contains detailed professional bio and contact information. A secondary column to the right appears to show testimonials or work samples, partially cut off. The palette is off-white and black, with a clean, serif-heavy typographic system.

title: Mid-century modern home office with extensive bookshelves
description: A home office or study corner featuring floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves lining a concrete grey wall, densely packed with books and interspersed with various sculptural objects and artifacts. In front of the shelves sits a mid-century modern wooden desk with a black chair, flanked by a classic black leather Eames lounge chair and ottoman in the foreground.

title: Sunlit Rustic Kitchen Corner with Wooden Furniture
description: A sunlit interior corner of a rustic kitchen or workshop, likely in Japan, with warm afternoon light streaming through a window with translucent screens. A weathered wooden counter and a worn table occupy the foreground, with a simple wooden chair tucked underneath. On the window ledge, small potted plants and ceramic vessels catch the light. The background reveals a cluttered but organized workspace behind a metal-grated window, with shelves, dishes, and a vintage lamp.

title: Loft bed over wooden dresser in compact apartment
description: A compact living space featuring a white-painted wooden loft bed structure positioned over a mid-century modern wooden dresser with multiple drawers. A pegboard wall organizer sits above the dresser, holding various small tools and items. To the right, clothing hangs on a rack attached to the loft structure. A ladder on the left provides access to the upper bunk.
ocr: IZEN GARDNER

title: Modern Loft Living and Music Studio Space
description: A spacious, industrial-modern loft interior combines living and studio areas. In the foreground, a white kitchen island holds various coffee-making equipment and containers. To the left, a music and work area is cluttered with percussion instruments, including cymbals and a xylophone, a large arched floor lamp, a wooden ladder, and various stands. The background features a living space with a long wooden dining table, chairs, a brown leather sofa, and a prominent white brick fireplace.

title: Industrial Loft Living Room with Book-Stacked Coffee Table
description: A spacious, industrial-style living room with white walls and exposed ceiling pipes. A large, low-profile coffee table is densely stacked with art and design books, serving as the central focal point. Behind it sits a plush, off-white sectional sofa. To the right, a large, sculptural paper floor lamp provides warm light, while a framed, dark-toned abstract painting hangs on the wall.

title: Modern living room with panoramic mountain view
description: A sun-drenched modern living room with expansive floor-to-ceiling glass walls framing a dramatic view of green, rolling mountain ranges. The interior features a plush, shaggy white rug laid over warm wood flooring. Furniture includes a light beige sectional sofa, a black armchair with a patterned pillow, a woven red pouf, and unique wooden and black geometric coffee tables. A large, dark architectural beam spans the ceiling. The overall feel is bright, airy, and connected to nature.

title: Bright industrial design studio with central table and Persian rug
description: A bright, industrial open-plan studio with high ceilings and exposed silver ductwork and pipes. The room is dominated by a long white rectangular table centered on a large, intricate Persian-style rug with a red and blue pattern. Around the table are mismatched chairs, including a white molded plastic side chair and wooden ones with striped upholstery. A large window with black metal frames looks out onto a neighboring building.

title: Concentric White Ovals on Dark Background
description: A graphic of concentric white ovals on a dark charcoal gray background. The ovals vary in thickness, creating a sense of depth and movement. The outermost oval is the thickest, while the innermost oval is the thinnest, giving the composition a target-like or ripple effect. The design is minimalist, with clean lines and a high-contrast color scheme.

title: Public Analog abstract blue graphic
description: A square graphic composition featuring a large, soft-edged blue shape resembling a blurry pill or capsule oriented diagonally from the top left to the bottom right. The shape has a deep navy blue core that fades into lighter cyan and eventually white at the edges, set against a light blue background. The entire image has a grainy, film-like texture, giving it an analog, nostalgic feel. The text 'PUBLIC ANALOG' is centered horizontally and vertically in a small, white, sans-serif typeface.
ocr: PUBLIC ANALOG®

title: Eclectic living room with modular shelving and gallery wall
description: A living room with ornate gilded ceiling molding against white walls. The main feature is a large, asymmetrical modular shelving system made of light-colored wood, densely packed with books and interspersed with drawers. Above it hangs an eclectic gallery wall of framed artwork and photographs. In the foreground, a low metal-frame coffee table holds a stack of books and a clear vase with pink and red ranunculus flowers. The floor is parquet wood, partly covered by a large pink rug.

title: Mid-century sunroom with glass roof and wood paneling
description: A modern sunroom extension with a steep glass roof supported by dark steel beams, overlooking a garden through a large picture window. The interior features light wood paneling and a multi-level wooden floor with built-in benches. The seating area includes a mid-century modern sofa with light blue cushions and two matching lounge chairs with curved wooden frames.

title: Geometric 'C' Logo in Construction and Final Red
description: Two versions of a stylized, angular 'C' logo shown side by side on a light beige background. On the left, a light gray version reveals its geometric construction with thin blue outlines and dotted guidelines. On the right, the final logo is a solid, bold red. The design is minimalist and geometric, with sharp angles and rounded ends on the open arms.

title: Mirrored Anime Screaming Star Faces
description: Two mirrored five-pointed stars are placed side by side, each filled with a close-up illustration of a screaming anime character. The left star contains a character with orange and blue elements, while the right features a character with blue, white, and orange. title: Zora IAMSOUND Digital Exhibition Press Release
description: A press release document from Zora announcing a collaboration with IAMSOUND for a digital exhibition called 'The Internet Renaissance'. The white page is centered on a dark, textured background with a soft purple glow along the left and right edges. The text is set in a clean, modern sans-serif font, with the Zora logo—a stylized geometric shape—prominently placed at the top left.
ocr:
Date: February 22, 2021.
To: Community
From: Zora
Subject: IAMSOUND x Zora
The Internet Renaissance is here. And it defies any labels, genres, or categorization.
We're excited to team up with IAMSOUND, a hybrid creative studio, record label and visual artist management firm, to reveal their latest exhibition of art on Zora. Over 20 of our favorite visual artists, musicians, and creatives have made eclectic, original works for this event, to be released onto the Zora protocol. Together, we're working on ways to push the boundaries of art. These talented people have helped us see the world in a new light.
Artists participating in this exhibition include:
Week 1 ACTUAL OBJECTS, CLARE GILLEN, JONATHAN ZAWADA, MURA MASA, ROSTAM, YAEJI
Week 2 BRYAN HUEHN, GUAPDAD 4000 X 88RISING, HASSAN RAHIM, IAMSOUND, SHAWN ELIAS, TORO Y MOI
This digital exhibition will forever be freely accessible to the public, while their ownership is singular. Owning a piece in this collection is like owning a painting by da Vinci or a statue in the halls of the Louvre. For the superfans, this can be your grail.
Ours truly,
(z)

title: Vermeer's Girl Masked by Nike Swoosh
description: A digital collage using the Nike swoosh logo as a mask or frame for a detail from Johannes Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring. The iconic swoosh shape is filled with a close-up of the subject's face, specifically her wide, gazing eyes and the textured, cracked oil paint surface of the original artwork. The composition is stark, with the black logo silhouette on a pure white background, creating a modern, commercial juxtaposition of a classic Old Master painting with contemporary branding.

title: Minimalist Hi-Fi Stereo System with Speakers and Records
description: A minimalist home stereo setup against a white wall with decorative molding. A low, open wooden and metal shelving unit holds a turntable, two silver-faced receivers, and two sets of vinyl records stored vertically. Flanking the unit are two large, dark brown wood-grain speakers on clear acrylic stands. Above the central equipment, a large framed concert poster is hung, and to its right, a smaller framed black and white portrait. The floor is a warm, polished hardwood.

The design consists of blurred, organic shapes and rings that continuously shift, creating a dynamic, noisy effect. The palette is limited to warm tones like orange, yellow, and pinkish-red, with occasional bright white highlights. The composition is centered within the square frame, giving it a pulsing, kaleidoscopic feel.

title: Understanding Minimalism article with index and references
description: A clean, text-heavy page titled 'Understanding Minimalism' defines the concept as minimizing distractions to focus on what is essential. The text explains how minimalism offers a direct view of a subject and finds application across many creative disciplines and lifestyle areas. Below the introductory paragraphs is a list of hyperlinks forming an index, followed by a references section with more links. The layout is simple and unadorned, with black text on a white background.
ocr: Understanding Minimalism Minimalism is defined as the concept of minimizing distractions from what's truly valuable or essential. As a result, a minimalist work offers a direct view at – and raises questions about – the true nature of the subject or object. It invites the viewer to consider it for what it really is: a shape, a thought, a movement—reminding us to focus on what's really important. Minimalism finds application in many creative disciplines, including art, architecture, design, dance, film making, theater, music, fashion, photography and literature. The minimalist principle also forms the core of a lifestyle movement and has made its way into sports, gastronomy, and many other areas. Understanding Minimalism explores these various disciplines one by one. DESIGN MACHINES

By Travis Gertz
July 15, 2015
Donald trawls Google Fonts for ten minutes. There are a few candidates, but Don's not so confident in his font evaluation skills. He lands on Open Sans. Good ol' faithful. He sets the actionable headline text to 48pt using the light weight in white. It's perfectly centred over the stock photo of anonymous hands fondling an electronic device. The semi-transparent overlay assures the marketing team that the headline will always be readable. Because who knows what the headline will be next month—or what stock photo will appear underneath.
Wait, we've seen this before. It looks hauntingly familiar.
The home page is due yesterday. The PM is lining up the next phase. The marketing team has been brainstorming headlines to A/B test. And if management can't jack up the ROI this quarter, winter's going to knock us back like the ice age. Let's play it safe and go with what we know works. Something

ocr:
Bartosz Ciechanowski
Blog
Archives
October 18, 2022
Sound
Invisible and relentless, sound is seemingly just there, traveling through our surroundings to carry beautiful music or annoying noises. In this article I'll explain what sound is, how it's created and propagated.
Throughout this presentation you will be hearing different sounds, which you will often play yourself on little keyboards like the one below. You can either click its keys with your mouse or use W E R keys on your computer keyboard, but before you do so make sure your system volume is at a reasonable level:
220 Hz
330 Hz
440 Hz
W
E
R
We'll eventually understand how these sounds are created and how they get to your ears, but we have to start by talking about the medium that is most commonly associated with sound – air.
Air
You're probably aware that at microscopic level air consists of individual, tiny particles. Let's look at the behavior of those molecules up close. In the demonstration below, I parcelled out a tiny cube of air – notice how the molecules freely enter and leave this space. You can drag the cube around to change the viewing angle and you can also control the speed of the flow of time with the slider:

ocr:
← Home
Refraction, dispersion, and other shader light effects
January 24, 2023 / 25 min read Last Updated: June 14, 2023
Since my very first lines of React Three Fiber and shader code, I've been obsessed with light and how to reproduce some of its physical properties to add some delight to my 3D scenes ✨. I gathered countless examples of renders featuring those effects in my inspiration board, but one of them that always struck me as incredible was chromatic dispersion.
Examples of dispersion effects by the Vercel Team, Davo Galavotti, and many other artists
Examples of dispersion effects by the Vercel Team, Davo Galavotti, and many other artists
While most of those are renders or use specific shaders to emulate the dispersion, I really wanted to see if it was possible to reproduce this light effect along with others on the web by staying as close as possible to the physics of light and how it interacts with a mesh while keeping it real-time. Despite the complexity of the problem and an increasingly deep rabbit hole, I've since then somewhat achieved this goal, and I'm going to tell you all about that in this blog post!

1. Intro
As a user, you need to interact with clickable UI elements like buttons, links, cards, and more.
If an action has a small target size, it will be harder for the user to click, or they might click an adjacent action element by mistake.
Let's take a look at the following example.
Menu
Try to hover on an item 👆
Notice the small target size? We can address this by increasing the target size.
When the target size is increased, it becomes easier for a user to click and interact with an element.
Menu

2. What is a target size?
The specific region within a user interface element where a user clicks, touches, or taps to trigger an action.

ocr: MMAP(BLOG) POSTS ABOUT ATOM FEED Enlightenmentware 2024-05-20 2024-05-20 UNIX Git Emacs Boost.Graph Bazel Conclusion As programmers, we interact with software tools daily. Most of them can barely get the job done. But occasionally, we discover a piece of software that transcends mere utility. These tools capture our imagination, open new possibilities, and affect how we design our own systems. I call such software enlightenmentware. The most common source of enlightenment for programmers is the programming language they use at work or learn as a hobby. I experienced many jolts of enlightenment from fiddling with programming languages, from MASM and C to Prolog and Idris. I won't focus on languages, however, since the effects of language learning on mind expansion is old news. In this article, I praise the software that contributed the most to my enlightenment. ocr:
ThePudding
THE MUSICAL DIVERSITY OF POP SONGS
In 2014, Snoop Dogg asked 50 Cent what he missed most about the past, when hip hop "was what it was." 50 Cent replied "authenticity," which led to Snoop's infamous imitation of today's rappers:
2 DAYS OF FUNK
ITUNES NOW
THAT'S WHATS WRONG RIGHT NOW
Play for Snoop's take on '14 rap music
In short, originality has given way to homogeneity, with artists copying whatever's in fashion (especially as rap music becomes today's pop music).
Regardless of whether Snoop is right, the same could be said of 1990s hip hop. Or 1980s pop (with pervasive synths/808 beats). Or 1960s rock, when the Beatles (and their sound) permeated radio. The music industry will ride a trend (if it sells), and hit songs converge on a style.
Is there something unique about today's hits—artists taking fewer risks and creating a narrower range of sounds?

Watch the Video The desktop computer hasn't changed much in the last 30 years. It's still built on windows, folders and mouse input. But we have changed. We now use smartphones and tablets most of the time, since they are much easier to use. The traditional desktop computer is struggling to adapt the simple interfaces of mobile devices while also keeping its focus on productivity. With people switching to mobile devices for mundane tasks, we have the opportunity to rethink the desktop computer with a focus on getting professional work done. Neo is a conceptual desktop operating system interface that is built for todays people, needs and technologies. Visualized below are ideas that were designed to be implemented in a web browser without the use of any plug-in. I have no intention of taking this beyond the concept stage. However, I am putting my work out there hoping that people build upon it. PANELS Your whole screen for easy multitasking. Neo shows your apps as panels. They fill the full height of your screen and are placed next to each other without overlap. You can have dozens of panels open and easily scroll through them to switch between apps. Or resize and move them to work with multiple apps side-by-side. Panels use screen space more efficiently and are a more elegant way to What's wrong with windows? Overlapping windows as an interface metaphor were invented over 30 years ago. Since then, the number and the complexity of how we use computers has increased dramatically. Windows are now inefficient and incompatible with modern productivity interfaces. Further reading

ocr:
systematically about how a product will work: the rules, the requirements, the edge cases, the annotations, the hard work.

(I think they don't tell you that in design school because most people would drop out.)

The truth is: You have to have a pretty systematic brain to be able to design digital products. Inspirational mood boards might look great on paper, but our job is to design products we can actually ship.

This is a visual transcript of my talk at Adobe Max 2021, How to (properly) break your design system. watch the video version on YouTube if you prefer.

REMEMBER WHEN I WAS 8, this quite vivid memory of my dad, who was an engineer at the time, designing the blueprint of our new home. I remember the smell of the graph paper he used, watching him meticulously draw with a green pencil and ruler. Once the foundations were in place, my father would color code electric wiring, water pipes, annotate wall and floor types, write instructions for the electrician, write special instructions for the builders, and so forth.

That was probably my first exposure to a Design System: a set of patterns and rules documented in such a way that other people could use to build something.

title: Dropbox Web Redesign Interface Mockup
description: A mockup of a modern, clean Dropbox web interface displayed on a white card against a solid light blue background. The interface features a sidebar on the left with navigation links and a main content area listing files and folders in a table format with columns for Name, Kind, and Modified. The layout is minimalist, using a palette of white, light grays, and Dropbox's signature blue. The overall feel is organized and professional.

Introduction Dropbox has created some amazing capabilities on the web that can change the way people work. However over the years we've outgrown the model of appending new features to a list. And we've made them difficult to adopt by designing each of them differently. The redesign of dropbox.com is about creating a design system for our web experience, which would reorganize and present all of our products as an accessible, focused, creative suite.

A4 + 180 mm A0 Format

Swiss Style The International Typographic Style, also known as the Swiss Style, is a graphic design style that emerged in Switzerland in the 1950s and 1960s. It is characterized by its use of grid systems, sans-serif typefaces, and a focus on clarity, readability, and objectivity. The Swiss Style has had a profound influence on graphic design and is still widely used today.

title: Jasper Morrison essay page with margins and text blocks
description: A white digital page displaying a long-form essay titled 'Super Normal' by Jasper Morrison. The layout is clean and minimalist, with left-aligned body text in a small sans-serif font. A narrow left margin contains metadata, including the author name, section title 'Essays', and publication details like 'Super Normal 2006 From Super Normal, published by Lars Müller Publishers'. The top right corner has a 'Menu' link and page indicator '<1/4>'.
ocr:
Jasper Morrison
Essays
Menu
<1/4>
I was having a cup of tea with Takashi Okutani in Milan, during the 2005 Salone del Mobile, talking about projects underway with Muji and describing to him the Alessi cutlery project and how I was feeling this approach of, letting off the design, seemed more and more the way to go.
I mentioned having seen Naoto Fukasawa's aluminium stools for Magis and how they seemed to have a special kind of normality about them, and he added, "super normal." That was it, a name for what's being going on, a perfect summary of what good design should be, now more than ever.
A while ago I found some heavy old hand-blown wine glasses in a junk shop. At first it was just their shape which attracted my attention, but slowly, by using them every day, they have something more than just nice shapes, and I notice their presence in other ways. If I use a different type of glass, for example, I get a feeling something is missing in the atmosphere of a dinner, and I may get a feeling that something is not right. These wine glasses are made of plain glass, and yet they radiate something good. Wine glasses as objects can seem to be full of something or empty, but the presence of a plain wine glass with its heavy spirit is the most mysterious and essential quality in objects. How can it be that so much effort is spent to have any real beneficial effect on the atmosphere, and yet these glasses, made without much design thought or any attempt to achieve anything better than a good ordinary wine glass, happen to be successful? It has been puzzling me for years and influencing my attitude to what constitutes a good design. I've started to measure my own designs against objects like these glasses, and not to care if the designs become less noticeable. In fact a certain lack of noticeability has become a requirement.
Meanwhile design, which used to be almost unknown as a profession, has become a major source of pollution. Encouraged by glossy magazine features, and marketing departments, objects seem to need things as noticeable as possible by means of colour, shape and surprise. Its historic and electric purpose is to sell things and the happy consuming masses at the same time, of course thinking it has to make and better to live with, seems to have gone side-tracked. The virus has already infected the everyday environment. The idea of businesses to attract attention provides the perfect carrier for the disease. Design makes things seem special, and who wants normal if they can have special?
And that's the problem. What has grown naturally and unselfconsciously over the years cannot easily be replaced. The normality of a street of shops which has developed over time, offering various products and trades, is a delicate organism. Not that old things shouldn't be replaced or that new things are bad, but that the things which are designed to attract attention are usually utilitarian. There are better ways to design than putting a big effort into making something look special. Special is generally less useful than normal, and less rewarding in the long term. Special things demand attention for the wrong reasons, interrupting potentially good atmosphere with their awkward presence.
The wine glasses are a signpost to somewhere beyond normal, because they transanced normality. There's nothing wrong with normal of course, but normal was the product of an earlier, less self-conscious age, and designers working at replacing old with new and hopefully better, are doing it without the benefit of that knowing normal demands. The wine glasses and other objects from the past reveal the existence of Super Normal, like spraying paint on a ghost. You may have a feeling it's there but it's difficult to see. The Super Normal object is the result of a long tradition of evolutionary advancement in the shape of everyday things, not attempting to break with the history of form but rather trying to summarize it, knowing its place in the society of things. Super Normal is the artificial replacement for normal, which with time and understanding may become reverted to being an everyday life.

title: Illustration for blog post on software and large language models
description: A blog post page with a pale yellow background and a two-column layout. On the left, a narrow sidebar features a small profile photo of a man, the name Geoffrey Litt, and a vertical list of navigation links. The wider main column on the right contains the article titled in large black serif type, with a subtitle and several paragraphs of text. A prominent illustration in the center shows a stylized robot and a human figure collaborating at a glowing computer screen filled with code.
ocr: March 2023 Geoffrey Litt Malleable software in the age of LLMs Projects Writing Inspirations Newsletter Twitter Mastodon RSS Email me All computer users may soon have the ability to author small bits of code. What structural changes does this imply for the production and distribution of software? It's been a wild few weeks for large language models. OpenAI released GPT-4, which shows impressive gains on a variety of capabilities including coding. Microsoft Research released a paper showing how GPT-4 was able to produce quite sophisticated code like a 3D video game without much prompting at all. OpenAI also released plugins for ChatGPT, which are a productized version of the ReAct tool usage pattern I played around with in my previous post about querying NBA statistics using GPT. Amid all this chaos, many people are naturally wondering: how will LLMs affect the creation of software? One answer to that question is that LLMs will make skilled professional developers more productive. This is a safe bet since GitHub Copilot has already shown it's viable. It's also a comforting thought, because developers can feel secure in their future job prospects, and it doesn't suggest structural upheaval in the way software is produced or distributed. However, I suspect this won't be the whole picture. While I'm confident that LLMs will become useful tools for professional programmers, I also think focusing too much on that narrow use risks missing the potential for bigger changes ahead. Here's why: I think it's likely that soon all computer users will have the ability to develop small software tools from scratch, and to describe modifications they'd like made to software they're already using. In other words, LLMs will represent a step change in tool support for end-user programming: the ability of normal people to fully harness the general power of computers without resorting to the complexity of normal

title: Potluck essay with interface screenshot
description: A clean, minimalist layout for a research essay from Ink & Switch, dated October 2022, authored by Geoffrey Litt, Max Schoening, Paul Shen, and Paul Sonnentag. The page features a main title and subtitle at the top left, followed by a multi-paragraph essay text. A large, central screenshot showcases the Potluck interface, split into two panes: an enhanced text document with recipe notes on the left and a computational environment with live search results on the right.
ocr:
Potluck
Dynamic documents as personal software
Today, personal computing is organized around apps: large prefabricated units of software developed by professionals for the masses, with few opportunities for customization. How might we reorient computing so that people can deeply tailor software to meet their unique needs?
We think a promising workflow is gradual enrichment from docs to apps: starting with regular text documents and incrementally evolving them into interactive software. In this essay, we present a research prototype called Potluck that supports this workflow. Users can create live searches that extract structured information from freeform text, write formulas that compute with that information, and then display the results as dynamic annotations in the original document.
We've found that Potluck is versatile enough to build personal tools for managing recipes, workouts, household chores, and more. We share some findings from building these tools, and envision a computational environment where these primitives help people grow documents into personal tools.

I'm also open to other kinds of design work, especially stuff that involves lots of text, including mini-sites and other web projects with special requirements (web books, community sites, etc). You're welcome to reach out and see what else we can work on together—custom, human-scale sites are what I'm good at.
To those creative people who say "I don't need a website," I ask: why not have a personal website that works strategically, in parallel to your other activities? How could a website complement what you already do rather than competing or repeating? How can you make it fun or thought-provoking or (insert desired feeling here) for you? How can the process of making and cultivating a website contribute to your approach?
...each artist should create their own space on the web, for a website is an individual act of collective ambition.
Chances are, you're coming to this page having seen my work before, and with a particular project in mind. In that case, you could skip straight to the Process section to read about what working with me is like.
▶ YOU SHOULD PROBABLY NOT HIRE ME IF...
the product
The best compliment for any piece of creation is often a single earnest "wow".
You want a really cool website. I'm assuming that's your primary goal. You want it to be nice to look at, great to read, make visitors whistle in appreciation, etc. etc. You want a site that is custom-built to match match the vibe of your project/personality/community.
I work with people to get a sense of their aesthetic and preferences, and then design sites that they wouldn't be able to dream up on their own. I've worked with descriptions like "Whole Earth Catalogue", "LaTeX paper" and "teenage engineering", and produced some of my best sites.
The most fun part of this process is when people start to see what's really possible outside of the current meta of standard blog themes. How you can have sidenotes and bookshelves and media hoards and cool new navigation patterns. What it feels like to design something in your image.

description: A screenshot of the Utopia website homepage. A central dark navy blue container features a large gold serif headline about scaling type and space, followed by three numbered steps in white text. Above the main content area, a navigation bar includes links for Type, Space, and Grid, among others. ocr: UTOPIA. FLUID RESPONSIVE DESIGN Type Space Grid Clamp Blog Showcase Merch Link Link Link Elegantly scale type and space without breakpoints Instead of tightening our grip by loading up on breakpoints, we can let go, embracing the ebb and flow with a more fluid and systematic approach to our design foundations 1 Define type and space scales for a small screen 2 Define type and space scales for a large screen 3 Tell the browser to interpolate between the two scales, based on the current viewport width @MIN @MAX SHOW SPACE Utopia emerges when designers and developers share a systematic approach to fluidity in responsive design. Instead of designing for x number of arbitrary breakpoints, we can design a system within which elements scale proportionally and fluidly. This can help you to: Design and code minimally and elegantly Streamline collaboration between design and development roles Ensure visual harmony and consistency Utopia is not a product, a plugin, or a framework. It's a memorable/pretentious word we use to refer to a way of thinking about fluid responsive design. Desktop Neo
rethinking the desktop interface for productivity.
Watch the Video
The desktop computer hasn't changed much in the last 30 years. It's still built on windows, folders and mouse input. But we have changed. We now use smartphones and tablets most of the time, since they are much easier to use.
The traditional desktop computer is struggling to adapt the simple interfaces of mobile devices while also keeping its focus on productivity. With people switching to mobile devices for mundane tasks, we have the opportunity to rethink the desktop computer with a focus on getting professional work done.
Neo is a conceptual desktop operating system interface that is built for todays people, needs and technologies. Visualized below are ideas that were designed to make the operating system more intuitive and efficient. I am not good at coding. I have no intention of taking this beyond the concept stage. However, I am putting my work out there hoping that people build upon it.
PANELS
Your whole screen for easy multitasking.
Neo shows your apps as panels. They fill the full height of your screen and are placed next to each other without overlap. You can have dozens of panels open and easily scroll through them to switch between apps. Or resize and move them to work with multiple apps side-by-side.
Panels use screen space more efficiently and are a more elegant way to
What's wrong with windows?
Overlapping windows as an interface metaphor were invented over 30 years ago. While the concept has stayed the same then, the complexity of how we use computers has increased dramatically. Windows are now inefficient and incompatible with modern productivity interfaces.

Responding to a user-hostile world
Design is inherently political, but it is not inherently good. With few exceptions, the motivations of a design project are constrained by the encompassing platform or system first, and the experiences and values of its designers second. The result is designers working in a user hostile world, where even seemingly harmless platforms or features are exploited for state or interpersonal surveillance and violence.
As people living in societies, we cannot be separated from our political contexts. However, design practitioners research and implement systems based on a process of abstracting their audience through user stories. A user story is "a very high-level definition of a requirement, containing just enough information so that the developers can produce a reasonable estimate of the effort to implement it." In most cases, user are grouped through shared financial or biographical data, by their chosen devices, or by their technical or cognitive abilities.
When designing for the digital world, user stories ultimately determine what is or is not an acceptable area of human variation. The practice empowers designers and engineers to communicate via a common problem-focused language. But practicing design that views users through a politically-naive lens leaves practitioners blind to the potential weaponisation of their design. User-storied design abstracts an individual user from a person of rich social and political agency to a collection of designer-defined generalisations. In this approach, their political and interpersonal experiences are also generalised or discarded, creating a shaky foundation that allows for assumptions to form from the biases of the design team. This is at odds with the personal affairs of each user, and the complex interpersonal interactions that occur within a designed digital platform.
When a design transitions from theoretical to tangible, individual user problems and motivations become part of a larger interpersonal and highly political human network, affecting communities in ways that we do not yet fully understand. In Infrastructural Games and Societal Play, Eleanor Saitta writes of the rolling anticipated and unanticipated consequences of systems design. "All intentionally-created systems have a set of things the designers consider part of the scope of what the system manages, but any nontrivial system has a broader set of impacts. Often, emergence takes the form of externalities — changes that impact people or domains beyond the designed scope of the system." These are no doubt challenges in an empathically designed system, but in the context of design homogeny, these problems cascade.

ocr: / ABOUT NOTES ESSAYS NEWSLETTER OFFSITE 27 May 2023 / San Francisco, California A calendar invite will appear with a cryptic note: a strange location attached — somewhere in the middle of nowhere up north, across the bridge — and a dozen or so people on your team will be subscribed. It might be bowling, or a visit to a farm, or a fancy dinner. There will be emojis and long threads and emails announcing the time and place. Sure, you'll go — you have to enjoy all this mandatory fun — and you hope it won't be awkward as the last time. Yet since no one wants to be there, it always is. You've found yourself trapped at a team offsite, and you can never escape. This is how a lot of tech companies think about team building and I've always loathed these exercises, not because I hate fun and never want to set foot on a farm ever again, but because they reveal a certain kind of naivety about team-making and building morale. I've always felt that great teams don't need day trips to wine country or mini vacations. Instead, the best team building exercise is to give folks good, worthwhile work. Honest work. What kills great teams isn't the lack of team offsites but the lack of focus, direction, resources, support, and financial recompense. A trip to the arcade or the bowling alley is incapable

ocr:
Annie Godfrey Larmon is a writer and editor based in Garrison, New York. Her essays, reviews, and interviews have appeared in apricota, Artforum, BBC Culture, Bookforum, CURA., Even, Frieze, MAY, the Miami Rail, Spike, Texte zur Kunst, Topical Cream, Vdrome, WdW Review and the White Review. The recipient of a 2016 Creative Capital | Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant for short-form writing, she was the editor of publications for the inaugural Okayama Art Summit and is a former international reviews editor of Artforum. As an editor, she has also worked on books for MoMA, MoMA PS1, Lévy Gorvy, and the Hessel Museum of Art. Godfrey Larmon has been a writer-in-residence at the LUMA Foundation in Arles, France; Mahler & LeWitt Studios in Spoleto, Italy; and Cuttyhunk Island Writers' Residency. She is currently at work on her first novel.

ocr: Article by Richard Ekwonye August 2023 Bézier curves have been a recurring theme in my frontend engineering career. I have used them extensively in my work - in animations and SVG paths of illustrations and icons. However, I only recently took an interest in understanding the underlying logic that governs their behaviour. This demystified curve-related path commands for me and gave me a deeper understanding of web animations. In this article, I'll share my interesting findings on Bézier curves. On a web page, we can render different types of images. The most common are .jpg, .png, .webp and .svg. SVG is unique because it is a vector image. While the others are raster. About Paul Budnitz owns and runs Budnitz Bicycles, a luxury bicycle company, Ello, a social network, and is well known as the founder of
Kidrobot, a toy company that produces designer toys and accessories. Budnitz is also an author of several books, exhibits as a photographer and filmmaker, and has founded over a dozen companies.
The son of a nuclear physicist and a social worker, Paul Budnitz was professionally coding safety analysis software for nuclear power plants by the time he reached high school. He also created video games for the now-legendary Commodore 64 home computer. By the time he was 20 years old he’d created more computer games than all other professional computer game ages combined.
Budnitz studied photography, sculpture, and film at Yale University, earning honors and a degree in Art in 1990. His first two films, 93 Million Miles and Ultraviolet, won awards in Berlin and many other film festivals worldwide. That first film, 93 Million Miles, and Ultraviolet, his second film, hailed 93 Million Miles as "one of the best films of 1998."
As Budnitz's energies became increasingly devoted to moving images, he became aware of gaps in existing technology. "Since there weren't any affordable ways to edit a film on a computer in 1995, I hacked my old Apple Mac, installed the first version of Avid Media Composer, and built one. In 1995 I made the first feature film to be edited on a home computer, an achievement chronicled in Wired Magazine in 1996."
That combination of entrepreneurial spirit, a keen aesthetic sense and encyclopedic love for global popular culture, and a well-developed talent for business, was to characterize all of Budnitz's future ventures, including Kidrobot.
"My grandfather was a small-town doctor and he used to say that I was missing a gene that told me that some giant risk I am about to take with my life is both stupid and dangerous. I'm grateful for this. Everything becomes more interesting if you get involved."
For Budnitz, one venture led organically to the next. He started his first business, M.O.B., while still in college, selling clothing he created to museum stores worldwide. This soon evolved into collecting, selling, and importing vintage clothing, such as classic Air Jordans and other wearable cultural artifacts, such as classic Air Jordans (which Budnitz sold in Japan for as much as $16,000 a pair).

#25, 01 Apr 2020
Quarantine: Day 27
I've been telling myself to journal more. But even though I value journaling and respect those who steadily practice it, I've always found it hard to form the habit for myself. However, I don't want to give up. In fact I've been inspired to keep at it after reading Jonnie's recent posts as well as the others coming through the RSS feeds I've been collecting and consuming. So I'm making an effort to contribute by sharing what's happening in our little corner of the quarantined world.

The kids are staying busy and have settled well into homeschooling. It's a mix of self-paced work and tasks which need our guidance. The school has them on Microsoft Teams where they distribute a daily work schedule and manage assignments as well as Zoom for teacher "office hour" chats and classmate "recesses". From 9-12 they focus on school. The rest of the day is split up into outdoor activities (the boys have started to build a fort), group activities like games/puzzles and some technology time (the new Xbox One is a hit).

My wife Cynthia and I fit in work hours when we can. She helps with accounting tasks for our church and gets most of those done at home, though one day a week she goes into the office to take care of needs which can only be processed on site. As for my work it has gone fairly uninterrupted. PCPartPicker started distributed so we've all returned to working alone, communicating via Slack and hoping on calls as needed.

This year I tasked myself to focus on a proper Design System for PCPartPicker so that work continues. In addition I'm diving back in to 3D, trying to keep my skills fresh and pushing myself into projects that feel just beyond where I feel comfortable. 3D is addicting and a nice change of pace from digital design work.

Outside of work and schooling we are maintaining our sanity by going on walks, bike rides,
playing board games, watching movies, and helping support local restaurants by ordering

Links to this note About these notes For now, there's no index or navigational aids: you'll need to find your own way in. I'll offer some starting point. You might be interested in §What's top of mind Athletes and musicians pursue virtuosity in fundamental skills much more rigorously than knowledge workers do Top-tier athletes are fanatically disciplined about improving their foundational skills—skills which transcend any sport, the same kind of agility drills you might see an army recruit do. Top-tier musicians do likewise: Lang Lang, for instance, is still working on his scales after 30 years as a concert pianist. They're not just doing rote drills: they're working to improve those skills critically, poring over performance videos and working with coaches. By comparison, knowledge work rarely involves deliberate practice. Knowledge workers rarely take those foundational skills seriously: fundamental skills like reading (People seem to forget most of what they read, and they mostly don't note it), note-taking (Noticing practices are ad-hoc and unsystematic, and if there are methods, they usually have no specific methods for developing skills over time). Core practices in knowledge work are largely ad-hoc, and knowledge workers have few tools or methods for developing skill in their core skills. I suspect that this is in large part because the possibility of improvement isn't salient. (Salience of improvement drives skill development.) What might it mean for knowledge workers to fanatically pursue virtuosity in the skills, in the ways that athletes seek in their fundamental skills? Ben Franklin practiced writing by taking an essay he found compelling and, without referencing it, rewriting it in his own words; then studying the differences in its language and his own. Susan Sontag 7/5/72 (As Consciousness Is Harnessed to Flesh: Journals and Notebooks 1964-1980) A writer, like an athlete, must 'train' every day. What did I do today to keep in 'form'? 2022-03-07 Interview with Pat Metheny in Believe, via Subtle Maneuvers. Metheny has a devotional relationship to music. He dismisses the idea of talent in favor of disciplined work, and is known for his practice discipline. He is obsessed with music: thinking about it constantly, performing over three hundred shows a year. For each one, he spends four hours in preparation. He avoids alcohol and sugar, and is critical of colleagues who are not as disciplined. After the show, he writes ten pages of notes on the performance, critiquing the sound, music, and audience, all in a series of Moleskine notebooks. He has never consumed alcohol or tried any drug, in order to stay focused on music.

ocr:
UX Principles
UX Principles
This is a growing list of UX principles that apply to our entire app. Last updated @ August 23, 2023
Principle 1
All icon buttons should have a tooltip on hover that says the full name of the function.
Principle 2
Any button that has a keyboard shortcut should have the keyboard shortcut in a tooltip on hover.
Principle 3
Every interactive item should have a hover state of some kind. When you move your mouse over the app, it should have the same kind of feel as if you just moved your hands over a control panel full of tactile buttons.
Principle 4
One primary call to action on every screen. There should only be one way to move forward and it should be clear. If there is no primary call to action, all the buttons should be secondary styles.
Principle 5
Primary buttons should always be in the same position within a flow. If you click a primary button in one place for 5 pages, the 6th page should have the button in the same place if it's part of the same flow.
Principle 6
Color is a distraction. If you can't get it to work in black, white and gray, color isn't the fix, it's a crutch. Yellow is acceptable in alert states. Red is only acceptable if something will be destroyed.
Principle 7
Do the hard work whenever possible. If there's something we can do for the end user, we should do it in the background automatically. Setting up a platform like ours can be a heavy lift, it should be weightless in our app.
Principle 8
Speed. No transitions longer than 150ms. Page loads should be instant.
Principle 9
We don't need it to be bells and whistles complete, but every feature we launch should work as expected in all use cases. We want to make an excellent knife instead of a shitty slap chop.

Concept
One of Resend's goals is to ship high-quality software quickly. This is crucial for the current stage of the company, so our design process is built based on these constraints.
We believe design is a discipline that can be exercised by anyone in the company. It is a way of translating user needs and business requirements into real solutions. This process can start with customer support, operations, or engineering.
Sharing taste and the meaning of quality is crucial for cultivating an open culture about design, and the key to achieving that is collaboration. It is very common for us to design solutions together, booking an hour to go through a problem and generate high-fidelity mockups in Figma together.
Here are the three phases the team can follow to design high-quality solutions:
Concept
The first phase is focused on navigating the complexity of the problem. The goal is to frame the problem, how we can solve it, what resources we need, and how we want the user to feel. It's a combination of research and play with the problem and the tools you have available: writing, coding, sketching, Figma, Retool, etc.

About
A Lot of Moving Parts produces 3D experiences for artists, architects, urbanists, and scientists, using research and computational tools to explore spatial representations, data visualization, and critical practice. The studio is led by Seth Thompson.
Collaborators
New York Review of Architecture, Ithaca College, Studio Museum, Institute School of Architecture, Johns Hopkins, City of Alexandria Office of the Arts, Sitedown, New Museum, Sitedown, SOPHia, Boucoup, Theo Anthony, MEMORY, Michael Jones McKean Studio.
Services
Interactive Spatial Design, 3D Visualization, Urban Data, Data Visualization, Film Web Development, Geospatial Research, Data Visualization, Film
We are interested in producing new ways of seeing the built environment, acknowledging that we are surrounded by complex spatial data, as instruments for making sense of the dynamic world around us. Our point of departure is the building, using techniques of modeling and simulation to present the entanglement between our ability to represent the world and how the world presents itself to us. These techniques are the result of our ongoing experimentation between the world and its representation. But at the ultimate test of a visualization is its ability to clarify and reveal its inner workings, or, as simply and effectively as a broad public audience.
Our process is iterative, collaborative, and occasionally conversational, reflecting the unique demands of each project and the creative forces of all involved. The studio operates in creative partnership with collaborators as early as the project cycle as possible. Depending on the scale of the project, the studio develops quick and efficient solutions, or projects that require the studio draws on the capabilities of a diverse group of partners. From our vantage point, a spatial visualization necessarily involves a lot of moving parts.
Twelve Earths
Details
Michael Jones McKean & Fathermens Art & Experiment, Norfolk, VA
With Michael Jones McKean Studio, aguila ochs, and Ana Goes.
Website
twelveearths.com >
Twelve Earths is a planetary sculpture initiated by Michael Jones McKean in collaboration with Morehshin Allahyari. The project centers on the story of a single, continuous path around the globe along a single line of latitude that connects a series of astronomical observatories in Chile and an ancient archaeological site in Portugal.
We designed an interactive website to document these locations and the various projects, artists, and artworks, using a wide array of multimedia, GIS research, astronomical data, and archaeological stratigraphy.

CHRISTOPH LABACHER
Interaction Designer
14. JANUARY 2020 [Updated 30. July 2022]
Colophon
About
Projects
Notes
Like that of many designers, my website used to be a portfolio of my work that I hadn't updated in years. At some point, I realized how much I miss the more personal websites people used to have. I want my website to be a place where I try things — and thoughts —, a playground for my ideas; not just my professional CV.
VISUAL DESIGN META
So in early 2020, I decided to start fresh and try some things I am interested in, like quirky minimalist typography and utilizing peripheral vision by reinterpreting marginal columns for the digital age. I decided to have some fun and take some risks: I made some controversial decisions on purpose. And if you are reading this, it means I don't hate it yet! — As a matter of fact, I did a rewrite of the website in 2022 and decided to change the design only slightly and focus on improving the typography and introducing some new content formats.
DESIGN
I do hope the combination of an absolutely minimalist set of stylistic devices combined with extreme precision and love for details ends up being powerful, rather than boring.
SPACING UNIT
One of the fundamental properties of any design is its smallest unit of spacing, from which all other spacings are derived.
Reading the book "Measure and Construction of the Japanese House" I recently learned the astonishing fact that the Japanese language once had a specific word for a measurement unit that is not defined as an absolute value, but simply as a uniform length that defines the rhythm of a building:

EDITORIAL / ESSAY
Notes on "Taste"
May 2, 2022
by Brie Wolfson
Gertrude Stein's home. [A black and white photograph of a room with walls covered in framed paintings, and ornate dining table, and a wood burning furnace.]
Taste is a word I've been hearing a lot more lately, and I think it's because we've broadened its application from the world of the aesthetic to the world of the practical. Taste has historically been reserved for conversation about things like fashion and art. Now, we look for it in our social media feeds, the technology we use, the company we keep, and the people we hire.
When I ask people what they mean by "taste" they'll stumble around for a bit and eventually land on something like "you know it when you see it," or "it's in the eye of the beholder." I understand. Words like taste are hard to pin down, perhaps because they describe a sensibility more than any particular quality, a particular thing. We're inclined to leave them unencumbered by a definition, to preserve their ability to shift shapes.
But I don't think we have to. And for the past several months, I haven't been able to resist the urge to try to articulate taste. This comes, in part, from a place of wanting to be precise — now that the term is such a frequent and varied part of our lexicon, it runs the risk of losing its meaning. But I also believe that doing so might unlock more than just the meaning of the word. Because taste itself is a virtue, per se, but because I've found a taste-filled life to be a richer one. To pursue it is to appreciate ourselves, each other, and the stuff

description: A vintage printed page from the Munsell Color System atlas, specifically Chart R, featuring a diamond-shaped grid of color swatches. MUNSELL COLOR SYSTEM
ATLAS
COLOR CHARTS.
COPYRIGHT BY A. H. MUNSELL 1907-1915
PATENTED JUNE 28, 1905.
CHART
R
SCALE OF VALUES
SCALE OF CHROMAS
RED AND BLUE-GREEN CHART.
This chart presents a variation in light and strength of two hues in complimentary hues, red and blue-green. The pair of opposite hues is shown in a regular balanced scale from black to white (V), and from grays to the strongest or most intense (C). These scales are independent of each other and so is the variation of the two hues. VALUES: red and blue-green range relatively from black or white to 10 (V). CHROMAS: or strength of the color range relatively from grays to 5/2. Red and blue-green, being complementary, must be present in the same quantity to produce a neutral gray (N). Each step in these color scales has an appropriate neutral gray in light and in strength. Thus R 15/ or 15/ variation, the corresponding gray is 5/N. The ratio of red to blue-green is indicated by the numerals to the left and right of the gray, e. g. 15/ means one (1) part of red to two (2) parts of blue-green. This does not mean a decrease in the amount of light lost but only 50% of chroma. To balance this pair the areas must be inversely as the chromas, i. e. since
blue-green is just half as strong as red and 15/ of red would require an area of 15/ of blue-green to balance it. In this chart the complementary hues are balanced by using their symbols, thus light blue-green (B25G) balanced by 2/15 red, 10/25 red by light red and twenty-four-four parts of dark red.
The MUNSELL ATLAS, page IV in the back cover, 'A Color notation', describes these balances that are needed to produce neutral gray of different degrees of light or dark. The symbol on each color step is its NAME, a measure of its light strength by which it is to be measured, related and reproduced.

The chart features a central circular grid with horizontal and vertical axes of color swatches. CHROMATIC BRANCHES OF THE COLOR TREE
(Color of pigment shadows (108)
CHROMA: i.e., the strength of pigment color or, the third dimension of value -- the other two being Value, i.e., brightness or darkness, and Hue, i.e., color name. The outer ends of the branches are more saturated and the inner ends fade to a neutral grey of the same value.
These branches are of various lengths and show different amounts of saturation. For example, the Red branch projects more than the Yellow.
The central vertical column (A) shows a neutral scale of grey values, from white at the top to black at the bottom.
The horizontal branches show different hues. The Green branch (left) has five steps of chroma. The Red branch (right) has eight steps. The Yellow branch (top) has four steps. The Purple branch (bottom) has five steps.
The circular outline suggests the 'color sphere' or 'color solid' concept.
These steps are not due to personal likes or guesswork, but have been scientifically established by the Munsell Color Company.
They represent the pigment colors in their purest state. The outer ends are 'true-bue,' not yellowed, nor faded. The inner ends are of the same value and hue but of less saturation.
Measured scales of VALUE and CHROMA make it possible to define a color with certainty.

description: A two-page layout for a French learning guide. The top section has a light cream background with a dark blue header reading 'Learn french in one year without the fluff.' Below is introductory text and three colored dots labeling 'Debutant', 'Middler', and 'Speakeasy'. ocr:
Learn french in one year without the fluff.
One year for going from zero to francophone on one page - in three parts because when learning french it's best to know from the beginning that there are many ways to create an exception.
Debutant
Middler
Speakeasy
WILL I EVER UNDERSTAND?
WILL CRY?

WHO WILL BE PROUD OF ME?

IS THIS EVERYTHING?
IS MY EGO GOING TO SURVIVE?

This is how you begin
3 MONTHS
A1
The first few months is your time to really grasp all the fundamentals of the language and stay accountable to absorbing yourself in it. This is your easiest time because it's going to fly as you learn hundreds of new things your brain is quickly integrating. But it will also feel painful every time you stumble (and you will stumble over and over again) trying to recall how to say the most basic things and encouraging your brain to remember word orders and conjugations. Your teacher will take you through the necessary structures. Teacher not in the budget? Pick up an A1 - A2 grammar book with activities and make your way through to understand some fundamentals.
Learning a new language as an adult is fucking hard work so you need to hold yourself accountable until it's a habit. This is particularly important while you're not speaking in your new tongue because it's incredibly easy to fall back to the comfort of our own languages and habits. The easiest way to handle this is to give yourself a system. I'm a fairly relaxed person and not into much non-work structure but you need a structure for this. It makes it achievable to get through your year.
I created a Notion database to track my learning time across each activity. Download my template to do the same for yourself. If you prefer hanging stuff on the wall or fridge, I've made a PDF for so download that instead. Or use these as examples

I purchased the LG C9 OLED right when it came out in 2019. It's ridiculously thin. So much so that you're going to be paranoid about breaking it when you unbox it or try to move it to a new house. It's been amazing and I would get it again in a heartbeat. It's more than 5 years old now and I haven't had any issues at all.

OLED TVs known for extremely high contrast levels, deep blacks and vibrant colors at the expense of not being as bright as LED-backlit TVs. This makes it less than ideal for viewing in bright rooms. OLEDs also have the potential for screen burn-in. I can see that briefly at times when the Apple TV home screen is left on the screen for a while but it is extremely faint and goes away.

About > Design
Design
In lots of ways, Blot is hidden. Most of the time, people who use Blot do so without looking at it. They simply edit the folder.
Some things however, are visible. The templates, which I am yet not proud of, are an example of this.
Aesthetic considerations one of my main motivations to work on Blot.
I find almost all of the internet deeply ugly. My interests in type design lead me to study the work of the early printers, and I find their books to be intensely beautiful. It upsets me that though we are decades into the internet, it remains generally ugly.
I find old books, especially Italian ones made by early printers, to be very beautiful. I like objects that can age and break and be repaired with dignity. I like medieval buildings and I don't think that ornament is always a crime. I like things which can be handed down, things that have been handed down. Old books taught me that beauty is a prophylactic for destruction.
Emojis: I dislike emojis partly because they look childish but mostly because their design is controlled by a corporation. See the pistol emoji for reference; on some platforms it appears as a gun, on others a water pistol. I love text.
SAAS aesthetic: Three-column pricing pages, enquire for enterprise rates, live-chat popups: "How can we help?", a team page filled with grinning teeth at the biannual beach retreat.
Calming
A lot of software makes me less calm. I want Blot to make more more calm, or at least not less calm.
Black or white backgrounds
Almost every website has a white or light background. So, Blot has a light background. It feels familiar. However, I do sometimes wonder about inverting the color scheme.
I like how David Rudnick justified the black backgrounds of his work. To paraphrase - the way computer screens work is they emit light, and that digital artifacts are light, in lots of ways.
I also spend most of my day in a text editor with a dark background, and find it comfortable on the eyes.
All of Blot's themes can be toggled from white to black with a single click on the template editor. Perhaps one day I will switch everything from white by default to black by default.

The New York Times
THE YEAR IN ILLUSTRATION
2017
Every year The New York Times commissions thousands of original illustrations from independent artists around the globe. Artists are asked to distill the most compelling aspects of stories and create a powerful experience. They often have just hours to make images that move, provoke and enrich the act of reading.
During years of tumult and uncertainty, illustrators use the medium's inherent flexibility to comment on a rapidly evolving social, political and economic landscape. When a single subject dominates the news, artists find new ways to elaborate on it without succumbing to dull repetition. They clear away the noise and get to the point, using pen, pencil, brush, stylus, cut paper, clay, motion and raw code to produce indelible images that resonate.
