title: Academic research paper on AI-enhanced interactive textbooks
description: A single-page academic paper with a dense, two-column layout typical of a conference proceedings. The paper is titled 'Balancing Efficacy and Engagement in Interactive Texts' by Jonah Bard from Dartmouth College. The text is black on a white background, set in a serif font (likely Times New Roman or similar), with clear section headings in bold.
ocr:
Balancing Efficacy and Engagement in Interactive Texts
Jonah Bard
Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH 03755, USA
Abstract
We introduce Phonopon, a digital learning platform that integrates LLM-graded formative assessment directly into reading materials. Through a randomized controlled trial with 11 students (11 in treatment, 5 in control) at Dartmouth College, the deployment of the Phonopon material was associated with an increase in final exam performance of between 8.71 SD (accounting for prior exam scores) and 13.50 SD (unadjusted). Presented as part of a follow-up study in a large lecture course, our study involved 113 students, 58 in treatment, and 55 in control, finding no significant difference in final exam performance. Additionally, score scores reveal a natural variation in student engagement. A human evaluator rated 20% of the LLM-generated questions, and found that the quality of the questions was acceptable, while also confirming that the corrected-repurpose question generator is a valuable tool for driving student success. We also discuss implications for the design of AI-augmented instructional tools.
Keywords
intelligent textbooks, large language models, formative assessment, intelligent tutoring, retrieval-augmented generation, reading engagement, corrected-repurpose assessment
1. Introduction
Now is the best time in history to be working on personalized instructional software. With the advent of LLMs, every student has a 24/7 knowledgeable personal tutor in their pocket. But if a basic LLM is all students need, why isn't academic achievement suddenly skyrocketing?
It appears that unassisted, external AI is largely a hindrance to students despite its convenience. In one experiment, students given unlimited access to GPT-4 actually harmed subsequent performance by 17% when the tool was removed – students used it as a crutch rather than a learning aid. A version of AI with carefully designed pedagogical guardians mitigated these negative effects. Meanwhile, student use of generative AI for academic work has been reclassified as academic dishonesty at many universities. At Dartmouth, 90% of students support using generative AI in educational settings, but only 53% of students report using it for studying, with usage rates decreasing from 53% just two years earlier [2].
Against this backdrop, it is well documented that university students are chronically under-reading their textbooks. Research has consistently shown that students read less when they move from a paper textbook to an ebook: from the 1990s, with students actively resisting reading assignments, and objective measures consistently showing substantially lower comprehension than students' self-reports [3]. In our deployment, student-reported completion rates for MATH 101 were approximately 35%, with instructors estimating 10%. Individual student behavior may vary from these estimates.
These observations motivated the design of Phonopon (also known as 'Pong'), a digital learning platform integrating LLM-powered formative assessment into interactive content. Phonopon embeds quizzes into the reading workload, making active reading a structural feature of the learning experience. The core premise is that AI is most effective when integrated directly into the core delivery of learning materials, rather than as a separate, bolt-on tool. This idea is supported by the well-documented 'door effect', in which completing practice questions interspersed into readings yields several times the learning impact of reading alone [4].

ocr: Feed Index de Wilde NYT Cooking From 2013-2017, I led product design for NYT Cooking, a new subscription digital product at the New York Times. My design director managed a cross functional team including design, UX research, product, project management, editorial, and engineering. title: Defining Taste Essay by Mitchell Hashimoto
description: A screenshot of a long-form text post by Mitchell Hashimoto titled 'Defining Taste'. The text is set against a plain white background in a clean, legible sans-serif font. The header displays the author's profile picture, name, handle, and verification badge, followed by the bold title and engagement metrics. The body consists of several paragraphs discussing the concept of taste, its value in the age of AI-driven production, and a personal note about writing the post in Apple Notes.
ocr:
Mitchell Hashimoto
@mitchellh
Defining Taste
144
608
4.2K
807K
"Taste" is the ability to consistently make high-quality qualitative judgments where no objective metric exists. It's the creation of something that feels right intuitively, with no real justifiable way to measure that. But when you do it, people feel it.
A person with "good taste" is someone who can do this repeatedly, consistently. The funny thing about taste is that it's hard to create, but its result is very easy to copy. Once someone makes a tasteful decision, others can imitate it almost immediately.
This is usually an argument against the existence of taste: "look how easy I can copy your work!" And yet, you couldn't create the work without first having someone to copy it from. One has taste, the other doesn't.
There have always been people with consistently good taste. But taste is coming up more regularly than ever before. It is becoming a critical differentiator.
For most of history, the ability to convert an idea to reality was itself valuable. Today, production is arguably rapidly becoming abundant. A single person with a defined vision (from anyone) can create what once required an entire team. This is, of course, largely driven by AI and partially driven simply by higher levels of abstraction.
Production is being commoditized much much faster than taste. It's an open question of whether AI will be able to produce "taste". For now, the ability to create qualitatively new judgments remains distinctly human.
Taste isn't valuable because it's impossible to copy. Taste is valuable exactly because it defines what everyone else chooses to copy. Taste has always existed! But now we value it more.
As always, I'll disclaim that this article was completely hand written. This time in Apple notes while I had no airplane WiFi!

I grew up in Durham, NC -> went to Durham School of the Arts and then Savannah College of Art and Design. Junior year I interned at Mekanism in SF, which really inspired me.
Post-college I co-founded an art collective and gallery space with friends back in Durham. Lots of art, music, and DIY events. Eventually I got restless with the south, worked my first agency job at Capstrat, then moved to SF and later LA.
I freelanced with some great studios -- B-REEL, Autofuss, BRKLY, NFLxSnapchat among them. At VICELAND I got to make title sequences and motion graphics for original shows alongside a wonderful team led by Dersu Rhodes, Eddy Moretti, and Spike Jonze.

title: Horizontal Scrolling Blog Post Layout Challenge
description: A clean blog post on a white background, headlined in large, bold, black sans-serif text: 'HORIZONTAL SCROLLING IN A CENTERED MAX-WIDTH CONTAINER.' Metadata above the title indicates a post date of March 11, 2022, and an 8-minute read time. ocr: Home Blog RSS Posted on March 11, 2022 Takes about 8 minutes to read HORIZONTAL SCROLLING IN A CENTERED MAX-WIDTH CONTAINER THE LAYOUT CHALLENGE When I had first assembled a gallery of CodePen projects to include on my personal site redesign in the summer of 2021, I imagined the following layout and interaction: • The page's main content container is centered on the page with a max-width set. • The first gallery item aligns with the left side of the content container. • Items overflow to the right and beyond the viewport, indicating that it can be scrolled horizontally. • Once scrolling is initiated, the left side of the gallery would break out of the content container, eventually sliding past the left edge of the viewport. This was a tough layout to get right! Ultimately, I decided to go with a slightly different homepage design that didn't rely on aligning the start position inside the page content area. In case my site design has been updated, this is for my future friends reading: You can see the aforementioned version of my site in this tweet from August 2021.

Beware the Permanent Periphery
Anton Leicht
Most countries will never have frontier AI. They're the ones who should be worrying.
Fear of AI disruption spreads in concentric circles. Outright frenzy inside the labs becomes intense distress in San Francisco becomes palpable anxiety on the East Coast — and once the sentiment has crossed an ocean, there's only mild discomfort left when it washes upon the shores of the other side.
An honest appraisal of the situation, however, should suggest the opposite response: It's the employees of the labs, rich in equity and embedded in the most dynamic labor market there ever was, that should feel the least apprehension. Though the institutions of American government face much more immediate disruptions, it is the periphery of AI development — the other 193 countries in the world without a domestic frontier AI developer to tax and regulate — that confront the biggest risks to their economic welfare and physical security.
These risks aren't resolved even if the AI built in San Francisco is particularly safe or particularly aligned. In fact, the risk may cut the other way: The better AI goes for its makers and their country, the more it threatens to disrupt the countries that build no frontier AI themselves. If their institutions, from labor markets to governments, are unprepared for the coming transition, their citizens risk being consigned to lasting irrelevance. They face life on the permanent periphery of a new world.
The other 193 countries
If you're reading this magazine, you too have probably been haunted by the specter of the "permanent underclass." The San Francisco Bay Area is abuzz with concerns that AI will irreversibly calcify a stratified economic order.
Their concern trades on a fairly specific set of premises: AI progress will continue unabated, and perhaps even accelerate. The American frontier developers that reap most of the ensuing economic gains. And the end point of this progress will be a radical transformation, where AI comes to dominate economic affairs and strategic statecraft and power accumulates for those

Getting a Taste of Startups

Los Angeles, CA

News
Space shuttle Endeavour traveled through Los Angeles streets to its new home at the California Science Center.
By the end of my mobile-agency years, I felt I had reached the ceiling of the opportunities available to me in Tampa and set my sights on the West Coast. The problem was that I had no idea how to get a job across the country. So, I improvised. I used Google Voice to give myself a California phone number and began applying to jobs on the west coast. When Mopro, a small startup in Santa Monica, invited me to interview, I instantly took on the opportunity. Although I had my sights set on San Francisco, Los Angeles gave me an open-ended first step into the technology world happening out west.
Mopro operated alongside Mohawk Digital as two parts of the same company. Mohawk Digital was a design and engineering shop, working with clients like QVC, Diesel, and The Economist. Mopro was the in-house product: a one-stop shop for small businesses to develop their online presence, including a website builder, commerce, and online-presence platform. The agency work helped fund the product, so I moved constantly between serving a particular client's needs and building a reusable system that could serve thousands of very different businesses.
Mopro became the internal project I was proudest of. We designed it during a period when skeuomorphic detail still shaped digital products, and we placed a heavy emphasis on visual craft throughout the experience. The product's meticulous execution became a clear demonstration of my visual design abilities.
It was my first close look at startup product development and my first experience translating an ambitious founder's abstract direction into concrete design decisions. I learned how to absorb strong opinions, find the useful intent inside them, and turn disagreements into forward motion.
It was also my first experience managing designers. I was young and suddenly responsible for hiring, motivating, and directing people who were often at the same stage of their careers as I was. Most of what I learned came through trial and error: how to make expectations clear, how to critique the work in a way that strengthened the person, and how to create enough trust for people to take creative risks.

title: Green Monoblock Chair Design Infographic
description: An infographic poster about the history and design of the iconic monoblock plastic chair. A green chair is positioned centrally against a white background, featuring a large gradient blur overlay. The composition uses a digital selection square effect, with thin blue lines and anchor points framing the chair. Bold green typography spells out the title, while several paragraphs of smaller text provide historical context.
ocr:
MONO BLOCK CHAIR
The monoblock chair was born in the 1960s, when engineers and designers began experimenting with the idea of shaping an entire chair from a single piece. Cheap, lightweight, and easy to produce, it quickly spread across the world. Today, the monoblock is both loved and joked about, a symbol of practicality and simplicity.
For decades, the monoblock chair has stood as the symbol of accessible design. Simple, durable, and instantly recognizable, it finds its place in parks, cafés, homes, and rooftops. Its story is one of innovation transformed into universal convenience.
The monoblock chair belongs to no one and to everyone. Born in an era of mass production, it became a silent protagonist in everyday life. It has been present at family gatherings, street markets, and grand celebrations without effort, becoming a quiet global symbol of unpretentious simplicity.
One piece. One mold. One idea that changed outdoor seating forever. The monoblock chair didn't become a phenomenon by standing out; it became one by being everywhere, appearing in millions of homes, streets, and events. It is the kind of object that became iconic simply by being everywhere.

title: Defining Taste essay by Mitchell Hashimoto
description: A screenshot of a long-form social media post or tweet thread by Mitchell Hashimoto titled 'Defining Taste.' The composition is a vertical column of text on a light gray background, with a user profile icon and handle at the top. The text is dense, sans-serif, and primarily black, with engagement metrics (likes, reposts, views) displayed in smaller, gray text. The essay discusses taste as a qualitative, human ability in the age of AI, arguing it is a critical differentiator.
ocr:
Mitchell Hashimoto
@mitchellh
Defining Taste
144
608
4.2K
807K
"Taste" is the ability to consistently make high-quality qualitative judgments where no objective metric exists. It's the creation of something that feels right intuitively, with no real justifiable way to measure that. But when you do it, people feel it.
A person with "good taste" is someone who can do this repeatedly, consistently. The funny thing about taste is that it's hard to create, but its results very easy to copy. Once someone makes a taste decision, others can imitate it almost immediately.
This is usually an argument against the existence of taste: "look how easy I can copy your work!" And yet, you couldn't create the work without first having someone to copy it from. One has taste, the other doesn't.
There have always been people with consistently good taste. But taste is coming up more regularly than ever before. It is becoming a critical differentiator.
For most of history, the ability to convert an idea to reality was itself valuable. Today, production is arguably rapidly becoming abundant. A single person with a defined vision (from anyone) can create what once required an entire team. This is, of course, largely driven by AI and partially driven simply by higher levels of abstraction.
Production is being commoditized much much faster than taste. It's an open question of whether AI will be able to produce "taste." For now, the ability to create qualitatively new judgments remains distinctly human.
Taste isn't valuable because it's impossible to copy. Taste is valuable exactly because it defines what everyone else chooses to copy. Taste has always existed! But now we value it more.
As always, I'll disclose that this article was completely hand-written. This time in Apple Notes while I had no airplane WiFi!

title: Relaxed Radix Balanced Trees blog post layout
description: A long-form blog post or article discussing Relaxed Radix Balanced Trees as a data structure for immutable vectors. The layout is a single column of left-aligned, sans-serif text on a white background, with generous line spacing. The content is divided into sections with uppercase headings like 'MERGING PERSISTENT VECTORS' and 'RELAX'. Near the top, there are three small, simple diagrams illustrating a tree merging operation, using boxes and connecting lines in green, yellow, and black.
ocr:
Peter Horne-Khan
Jan 8, 2024
Relaxed Radix Balanced Trees
I'm adding immutable vectors to my language, Ivan, and needed to pick a suitable data structure to implement them. Clojure uses Persistent Vectors (PVs) which support lookups, updates, and appends all in 'effectively' constant time. However, it doesn't have efficient insert or merge operations. Relaxed Radix Balanced (RRB) Trees, introduced by Bagwell and Rompf in 2011, address this shortcoming.
I had to read a few different papers to properly understand how they worked so I could also explain them in the hope of making it easier for others. I'll try to convey how they work and intuition for why, while leaving the deeper mathematical treatment to the academic papers.
I will assume you're already familiar with how Persistent Vectors work.
MERGING PERSISTENT VECTORS
Let's suppose we merge two Persistent Vectors, giving us the following result:
Since we rely on a fixed node size (M) for radix search to work, we must ensure that every node (except the right edge) has M children. A tree with this property is said to be leftwise dense. In this example, since the left child of the right vector only has 3 children, we have to repeat the merging process starting at the leftmost child of the right vector. Doing so imbalances the first child node of the right vector, so we must repeat the process with its subsequent children until all nodes are balanced. This process involves creating many new replacement nodes (shown in yellow). The work that needs to be done is proportional to the size of the right vector.
RELAX
We need to relax the leftwise dense constraint, but doing so will introduce two problems:
1. Radix search relies on each node having the same fixed branching factor.
2. The height of the tree, which is what lets us claim 'effectively' constant operations, is bounded by the fixed branching factor.

messages and Google your documents. By splitting up our data, we
prevent any AI from truly knowing us as individuals. And by giving away
all control, we relegate ourselves to mindless drivers of engagement.
What have we gained from sharing our lives with Facebook? If data is the
new oil, where are our cars?

And, although the parameterization of functions and its subsequent parameter estimation are the primary workhorses in the function approximation of statistical learning, with deep learning specifically, we consider parameterizations of a very particular type. Recall, insofar as we view the architecture of the brain, then being parameterized by weights w and biases b where theta equals w, b. Such models f_theta(x) are referred to as deep neural networks, which we can start by training single layer networks comprised of perceptrons, mathematical models of neurons. The computational circuit of a perceptron is pictured below, in the left panel of Figure 1.3.1, where a perceptron produces a real-valued scalar y by taking the sum of x_i and weights w_i.

The perceptron f_theta is a weighted sum of x_i's and w_i's, which can be rewritten as the dot product of the two vectors x and w. Such a dot product translates to torch.borcht.dot().
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
class Perceptron(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, d):
  super().__init__()
  self.w = torch.randn(d)
 def __call__(self, x: torch.Tensor):
  return torch.dot(self.w, x)
model = Perceptron()
y = model(x)
print(y)

title: Interface Design quotes from The Stack, Ben Bratton
description: A dense text document from a design research project, set on a black background with white type. The phrase SOFTWARE DESIGN AS ARCHITECTURE runs vertically down the left margin in spaced capital letters. At the top, a small justified paragraph quotes Benjamin H.
ocr: SOFTWARE DESIGN AS ARCHITECTURE "Perhaps today no discipline has more expertise in interface design than architecture, and perhaps someday no discipline will ultimately have more expertise in architecture than some expanded interdisciplinary mode of interface design, because for the City layer, computation is not privileged over sensing. The interfacial operations of software and architecture could easily be understood as two distinct and complementary but also mutually involved sides of corresponding governing efficacies sometimes symbolic and sometimes pragmatic in their operations. However, under the interfacial conditions of planetary-scale computation programs that we may have asked architecture to host in the past are now assignments for software, with the latter not only absorbing but sometimes hollowing out the former as well. Meeting rooms become chat windows, store shelves become online databases, places become geotagged, organizational hierarchies become firewalled User access configurations, and so on. This transformation doesn't only dissipate architecture's authority (though in some instances, it does exactly that). Nevertheless, because architecture works as collective interface to urban space and because computation draws our attention to interfaciality and its contested governance of systems, then how architectural design will continue to enforce programmatic authority becomes an increasingly pressing question. Architecture's ability to represent systems (idealized, abstracted, mythical, logistical) exceeds any physical mediation of space, and extends its reach beyond the semiotic play of the GUI at hand. At the same time, a shift in design discourse away from symbolization, toward direct material effect, and on political positions that are imminent in a structure's postural embodiment in location, also has to be seen as a disciplinary reaction to the challenges posed by software's virtualizations of architecture's heavier interfaces. It is a way of taking stock of what is left." (Benjamin H. Bratton, "The Stack: On Software and Sovereignty", 166) Interface Design 1. "Interfaces are thresholds. They connect and disconnect in equal measure, structuring flows by combining and segmenting it, enabling it or frustrating it, bridging unlike forms over vast distances and subdividing that which would otherwise congeal on its own." (228) 2. "[Interfaces] necessarily limit the full range of possible interactions in a specific and arbitrary way. Any interface, because it is a specific summary, must eliminate or make invisible a whole range of other equally valid possible interactions. [...] Only because they reduce and simplify complex systems can they make it possible for people to use those systems at a systematic scale and realize value from them." (221) 3. "[Interfaces] must reduce and conceal the complexity of the processes they represent." That reduction is also necessary to their ability to function as broadly useful social tools. (234) 4. "Further, as interfaces are reductive in how they compress information—in their foregrounding of certain things and not others—they are also inevitably 'ideological.' Their reduction toward resolution is doctrinal." (234) 5. "While interfaces fix and limit possibilities, they simplify them in different ways

title: Black starburst sparkle icon collection
description: A grid of sixteen black starburst icons on a plain white background. The collection includes four-pointed stars with sharp tips, multi-pointed bursts of varying numbers of rays, and small accent dots or crosses near some primary shapes. All forms are high-contrast black silhouettes, arranged in a four-by-four grid with consistent white spacing, creating a clean set of sparkle, glint, or star motifs for graphic design.

title: Mid-Century Japanese-Influenced Living Room with Vaulted Ceiling
description: A spacious mid-century modern living room with a vaulted, textured concrete ceiling and polished hardwood floors. The room is bathed in natural light from a large wall of windows with shoji-style screens, some open to a view of green trees. Key furniture includes a long, low wooden coffee table, a dark wood armchair with a white cushion, and a lounge chair in the distance. A large white paper lantern hangs from the ceiling, and a blue-and-white koi nobori flag stands vertically near the window.

title: Elderly Couple Working in a Sunlit Modern Living Space
description: A wide, eye-level shot captures a modern, open-plan interior with two elderly individuals seated at a large wooden desk in the middle ground. A low, built-in wooden shelving unit in the foreground acts as a room divider, filled with books, CDs, a vintage stereo system, and a large speaker. Above the desk hangs a large, horizontal abstract painting with muted tones, and a white paper lantern pendant light hangs centrally.
